sub: How a duct cell becomes an invasive cancer, and how genes, receptors and lymph nodes decide prognosis and the drug each patient gets.

pretest.q: Which gene is lost in invasive lobular carcinoma, letting the tumor cells spread in single file?
pretest.why: CDH1 encodes E-cadherin, the adhesion protein that holds epithelial cells together. Lobular cells that lose it no longer stick to each other, so they drift through the stroma one cell at a time and often involve both breasts.

w.ERBB2: ERBB2 encodes the HER2 receptor. Its amplification drives growth in about one in five cancers, mostly ductal, and does not change cell adhesion.
w.TP53: TP53 mutation is common in high-grade and triple-negative cancers and causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome, but it does not create the single-file growth pattern.
w.BRCA2: BRCA2 repairs double-strand DNA breaks. Its carriers develop mostly estrogen receptor-positive ductal cancers and male breast cancer, not a lobular pattern.

pretest.q: Which drug lowers estrogen by blocking its synthesis in fat after menopause?
pretest.why: Anastrozole is an aromatase inhibitor. After menopause most estrogen is made by aromatase in fat, so blocking the enzyme starves an estrogen receptor-positive tumor of its hormone.

w.Tamoxifen: Tamoxifen blocks the estrogen receptor in breast tissue but leaves estrogen production untouched. It works at the receptor, not at synthesis.
w.Trastuzumab: Trastuzumab is an antibody against the HER2 receptor. It treats HER2-amplified tumors and has no effect on circulating estrogen.
w.Fulvestrant: Fulvestrant binds the estrogen receptor and causes its degradation, so it removes the receptor rather than lowering estrogen synthesis.

pretest.q: Which screening mammogram finding is most typical of ductal carcinoma in situ?
pretest.why: DCIS cells fill the duct, and the cells in the center outgrow their blood supply and die. The dead debris calcifies, so clustered microcalcifications are how most DCIS is found.

w.Spiculated mass: A spiculated mass reflects invasive carcinoma pulling on surrounding tissue through desmoplasia. DCIS has not invaded and rarely forms a mass.
w.Smooth oval mass: A smooth, well-circumscribed oval mass suggests a benign fibroadenoma or cyst rather than ducts filled with carcinoma in situ.
w.Diffuse skin thickening: Diffuse skin thickening with redness points to inflammatory carcinoma, in which tumor emboli block the lymphatics of the dermis.

body: Who is at risk, and why does estrogen matter?

Breast epithelium divides each time estrogen rises during the menstrual cycle, and every division is a chance to copy a DNA error. Anything that adds cycles or estrogen therefore raises risk. Examples are early **menarche**, late menopause, nulliparity or a first birth after 30, obesity after menopause (fat makes estrogen through aromatase), combined hormone therapy and alcohol. **Dense breast tissue** adds risk and also hides tumors on a mammogram. Chest radiation in youth and atypia on an earlier biopsy raise risk further, while **breastfeeding** lowers it, partly because it suppresses ovulation.
Which genes and family histories raise risk?

About 5 to 10 percent of breast cancers are hereditary. {{rp24_brca|BRCA1 and BRCA2}} encode proteins that repair double-strand DNA breaks by **homologous recombination**. They follow the **two-hit** model. A carrier inherits one defective copy in every cell, and a breast cell becomes cancerous when it loses the second copy. Both genes also raise ovarian cancer risk.
BRCA1 and BRCA2 make different cancers

**BRCA1** carriers tend to develop high-grade, triple-negative (basal-like) cancers, often with a medullary pattern, plus high-grade serous ovarian cancer. **BRCA2** carriers tend to develop estrogen receptor-positive cancers and carry the highest risk of male breast cancer. Pancreatic and prostate cancers also cluster in their families.
Other inherited syndromes each come from a gene with a normal job, and losing that job explains the cancers.
Cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis after DNA damage
Li-Fraumeni syndrome: early breast cancer, sarcoma, brain and adrenal tumors
Cowden syndrome: breast, thyroid and endometrial cancer
Lobular breast cancer and diffuse gastric cancer
Kinase that restrains growth through AMPK
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: polyps, pigmented lips, breast and gut cancer
Partner of BRCA2; DNA damage signaling
Moderate increase in breast cancer risk
How does a normal duct become an invasive cancer?

Most breast cancers, ductal and lobular alike, arise in the terminal duct lobular unit, where a terminal duct opens into the milk-producing lobule. Its ducts have two cell layers, inner luminal cells and outer {{rp24_myo|myoepithelial cells}}, resting on a **basement membrane**. Carcinoma in situ stays inside the basement membrane, so it cannot reach lymphatics or blood vessels. Invasion begins when tumor cells cross the membrane, and the stroma responds with scar-like **desmoplasia**.

Cancers of this unit are thought to follow a **precursor** sequence. On the ductal side it runs from usual ductal hyperplasia to atypical ductal hyperplasia, then to ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and invasive ductal carcinoma. On the lobular side, atypical lobular hyperplasia leads to lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) and invasive lobular carcinoma. Usual hyperplasia is a benign, mixed population of cells, whereas atypical hyperplasia and DCIS are made of uniform cells.

DCIS fills and stretches ducts with malignant cells in solid, **cribriform** (sieve-like) or papillary patterns. In the high-grade **comedo** pattern, the central cells outgrow their blood supply and die, and the dead debris calcifies. So DCIS usually appears as clustered **microcalcifications** on a screening mammogram, not as a lump. LCIS is different. Its cells have lost E-cadherin, so they are small, round and loosely attached. They rarely calcify, so LCIS is usually found by accident on a biopsy done for another reason.
Incidental finding on a biopsy; usually invisible on mammography
Can become invasive ductal cancer in the same breast if untreated
Marks risk of invasive cancer in either breast, often ductal
LCIS is a risk marker, not a lesion to chase

Because LCIS predicts cancer in **both breasts**, removing the biopsy site does not remove the risk, and the cancers that follow are often ductal. LCIS is therefore managed by surveillance and chemoprevention, while DCIS is excised because it can become invasive where it sits.
Which invasive type is it, and what does each look like?

**Invasive ductal carcinoma** (no special type) is the most common, causing about 70 to 80 percent of cases. Its desmoplastic stroma makes a hard, stellate mass. **Invasive lobular carcinoma** carries the same CDH1 loss as LCIS, so its cells infiltrate in **single-file** rows without forming a discrete mass. It is more often bilateral or multicentric, can hide on a mammogram, and spreads to unusual sites such as the peritoneum, gut and ovaries. Most breast cancers arise in the upper outer quadrant, which holds the most glandular tissue, including the axillary tail. Men have ducts but no lobules, so male breast cancer is almost always ductal. It is usually ER-positive and linked to BRCA2 and Klinefelter syndrome.

Two presentations are recognized by what they do to the skin of the breast and nipple rather than by the tumor's cell type. In **inflammatory carcinoma**, tumor emboli plug dermal lymphatics, so the breast turns red, warm and swollen with dimpled **peau d'orange** skin, and the prognosis is poor. {{rp24_paget|Paget disease of the nipple}} is a crusted, eczematous nipple caused by carcinoma cells that spread into the epidermis from an underlying DCIS or invasive cancer. The table compares all the invasive types.
Set by grade, receptors and nodes
Syncytial sheets of large cells with lymphocytes
Cell nests floating in lakes of mucin
How do receptors decide prognosis and treatment?

Every invasive cancer is tested for the **estrogen receptor** (ER), the progesterone receptor (PR) and {{rp24_her2|HER2}}. The test is immunohistochemistry, a stain that shows each protein in the tumor cells. An equivocal HER2 result is settled by in situ hybridization, which counts copies of the ERBB2 gene. Each result is a drug target. ER and PR predict a response to endocrine therapy, and HER2 predicts a response to anti-HER2 drugs.

Gene expression profiling sorts invasive ductal carcinoma into four molecular classes. **Luminal A** tumors are ER-positive, HER2-negative and slow-growing, with a low Ki-67 index. They respond to endocrine therapy and have the best prognosis. Luminal B tumors are also ER-positive but divide faster or carry HER2, so they often need chemotherapy as well. HER2-enriched tumors have ERBB2 amplification and respond to anti-HER2 drugs. Basal-like tumors, mostly **triple-negative**, lack all three receptors. They are common in BRCA1 carriers and young Black women, depend on chemotherapy, and have a poor prognosis.

HER2, encoded by **ERBB2**, is a receptor tyrosine kinase. When the gene is amplified, the crowded receptors pair up and switch on growth and survival signals. This makes HER2 a drug target at several points, as the steps show.
From ERBB2 amplification to targeted drugs
Extra copies of ERBB2 crowd the cell surface with HER2 receptors, which is what HER2 testing detects.
Crowded receptors pair up and their kinase domains switch each other on. Pertuzumab blocks this pairing.
The active receptor drives the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways, so the cell divides and resists apoptosis. The tyrosine kinase inhibitors lapatinib and tucatinib block the kinase inside the cell.

**Trastuzumab** binds the outer part of the receptor, blocks its signal and marks the cell for antibody-dependent killing by natural killer cells. Antibody-drug conjugates such as trastuzumab deruxtecan carry a toxic payload into the cell.
Two drugs, two kinds of heart damage

Trastuzumab has reversible **cardiotoxicity**. It lowers the ejection fraction by blocking HER2 survival signals in heart muscle cells, and the damage usually recovers when the drug is held. Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin kill heart muscle cells through free radicals, so their cardiotoxicity is dose-dependent and largely permanent. Echocardiography monitors both.

Endocrine therapy starves receptor-positive cancer of estrogen signaling, and the best drug depends on where the estrogen comes from. **Tamoxifen**, the usual choice before menopause, is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM). It blocks the receptor in breast but stimulates it in the endometrium and bone. It therefore raises the risk of endometrial cancer and venous thromboembolism, and it protects bone after menopause. **Aromatase inhibitors** (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) block the conversion of androgens to estrogen and are used after menopause. They cause bone loss and joint pain. Fulvestrant, a selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD), and CDK4/6 inhibitors are added in advanced disease. Raloxifene lowers breast cancer risk without stimulating the endometrium. PARP inhibitors such as olaparib kill BRCA-deficient cells, which cannot repair the DNA breaks that pile up when PARP is blocked.
Why do aromatase inhibitors work only after menopause?

Before menopause the ovary makes most estrogen under the drive of FSH and LH. An aromatase inhibitor lowers estrogen, the pituitary senses the fall and releases more gonadotropins, and the stimulated ovary overcomes the partial block. After menopause the ovary no longer responds, and most estrogen comes from aromatase in fat, which converts androstenedione to estrone. Blocking that enzyme removes nearly all of the remaining estrogen. A premenopausal woman can take an aromatase inhibitor only if her ovaries are also suppressed or removed.
What predicts outcome, and how is cancer found early?

Axillary **lymph node** status is the strongest single predictor of prognosis, because nodal spread proves the tumor can leave the breast. Tumor size, grade, receptor status and distant metastasis complete the picture. Breast cancer spreads first to axillary nodes and then to bone, liver, lung and brain. Screening **mammography** finds cancers before they can be felt. As of 2025, the USPSTF recommends a mammogram every two years from age 40 to 74 for women at average risk.

A small tumor with positive axillary nodes usually has a worse prognosis than a larger tumor with negative nodes. This is why sentinel lymph node biopsy is part of surgery. The first node draining the tumor shows whether spread has begun, and a negative sentinel node spares a full axillary dissection.

body.q: A BRCA1 carrier has triple-negative breast cancer. Which reasoning best explains why a PARP inhibitor helps her?
o: PARP inhibitors block estrogen synthesis, which drives the growth of triple-negative tumors
Her tumor cells lack homologous recombination, so blocking PARP leaves DNA breaks they cannot fix
PARP inhibitors bind HER2 on the tumor surface and recruit natural killer cells
The drug restores BRCA1 function, so the tumor cells regain DNA repair and stop dividing
body.why: PARP repairs single-strand DNA breaks. When PARP is blocked, those breaks become double-strand breaks during replication. Normal cells fix them by homologous recombination, but tumor cells that have lost both BRCA1 copies cannot, so they die. Her normal cells keep one working copy and survive. This is synthetic lethality: either defect alone is tolerated, but both together kill the cell.
